theme: The heavens declare; the law revives the soul
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 19. Notice the three movements: the voice of creation (vv. 1-6), the perfection of God’s word (vv. 7-11), and the prayer of a servant who asks to be cleansed and made acceptable (vv. 12-14).
settingTheScene: Psalm 19 is a psalm of David. C. S. Lewis called it one of the greatest poems in the Psalter. It joins two ways in which God speaks: through the heavens (general revelation) and through his word (special revelation). We read the first part earlier in connection with Paul’s use of it in Romans 10. Today we read it as a whole, as we move into Revelation, where the whole creation and God’s written word are central.
observation: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork” (v. 1).
“Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge” (v. 2).
“The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul” (v. 7).
“The precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart” (v. 8).
“More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb” (v. 10).
“Moreover, by them is your servant warned; in keeping them there is great reward” (v. 11).
“Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults” (v. 12).
“Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer” (v. 14).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with the sky: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork.” The created order is a continual testimony. “Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge. There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard.” Creation speaks without words and in every language, and “their voice goes out through all the earth.” In the heavens, God has set a tent for the sun, which rises like a bridegroom and runs its course like a strong man with joy. “There is nothing hidden from its heat.” This general revelation shows the power and glory of the Creator but does not tell us how to be saved. For that we need his word.

The second part turns to the word, with six names for it (law, testimony, precepts, commandment, fear, rules) and six effects. “The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple; the precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes; the fear of the LORD is clean, enduring forever; the rules of the LORD are true, and righteous altogether.” This is how the Bible works: it restores the weary, makes the simple wise, brings joy, gives light, endures forever, and proves true. “More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb.” The psalmist treasures the word more than wealth and enjoys it more than sweets.

The third part is personal. Having seen the glory of God in creation and in his word, the psalmist sees himself. “Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults. Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me! Then I shall be blameless, and innocent of great transgression.” The word is a mirror that shows sins we cannot see by ourselves. He asks for cleansing from the hidden and the willful. And he ends with a prayer that has been prayed by preachers for centuries: “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.”

The movement from the stars to the Scripture to the sinner is the movement of faith. We look up and see glory, we look into God’s word and see grace, and we look inward and see our need. In Revelation, the creation praises its Creator (4:11; 5:13), the book is opened, and the redeemer is the Lamb. The one who is our rock is also our redeemer.
connection: Romans 1:18-20 and 10:18 draw on creation’s testimony. Psalm 8, 33, and 104 also praise God in creation. Psalm 119:97-105 and Deuteronomy 4:6-8 praise the law. 2 Timothy 3:15-17 describes the use of Scripture. Hebrews 4:12 describes the word as living. Psalm 90:8 and 139:23-24 speak of hidden sin. Psalm 51:1-12 asks for cleansing. John 8:12 and 1 John 1:5 link light to God. Revelation 4:11 and 5:13 have creation praising God. Isaiah 41:14 and 44:6 call God redeemer.
application:
Step outside today and look at the sky. Let it speak. Tell God what it says to you about him.

Read one of the descriptions of the law (vv. 7-9) and pray for the effect you most need: reviving, wisdom, joy, or light.

Pray verse 14 before you speak or write something important.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for speaking through the heavens and through his word.
Ask him to cleanse you from hidden faults.
